power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. text.text: Background: Social contact surveys measure how individuals interact with each other, which directly influences disease transmission dynamics.

The COVID-19 pandemic substantially altered how people live and work, highlighting the need for up-to-date and sub-national estimates of social contact patterns to inform disease modeling and public health planning.
conducted an opt-in social contact survey of upper Midwest residents, with about 60% of participants drawn from Minnesota.
Participants reported all interpersonal contacts during the previous day, including the age of their contacts allowing for the analysis of mixing patterns.
Detailed demographic information about the participants was also collected, allowing for additional subgroup analyses of contact patterns.
Results: Participants in our sample had an average of 6.8 contacts per day (IQR: 2.0 -8.0), which is within the range of recent post-pandemic US national and European estimates.
Contacts varied across demographic groups, with those attending work or school in-person reporting the highest number of contacts.
Mixing across most age group pairs was a little lower than in comparable national survey except for younger age groups, who had substantially higher rates of contact with same-age peers.
Differences in the contact matrices alone were associated with a 6.7% difference in estimated basic reproduction number(R0).
Near the epidemic threshold, even this modest difference could meaningfully affect transmission dynamics.

These effects may be amplified or attenuated by pathogen-specific age patterns of susceptibility and infectiousness, leading to larger or smaller differences in R0 estimates derived from national versus regional mixing patterns.

Conclusions: These findings provide empirical evidence on post-pandemic social contact patterns in the United States and highlight the potential implications of regional variation in social mixing for infectious disease transmission.
The mean 6.8 daily contacts is consistent with evidence of persistent changes in daily routines following the pandemic.
Incorporating contemporary, region-specific contact patterns into transmission models may improve their ability to capture geographic variation in transmission risk and inform epidemic forecasting.
Understanding how people interact and come into contact with each other is vital to understanding infectious disease epidemiology.
Erroneous assumptions about contact rates can lead to inaccuracies in mathematical model predictions, resulting in sub-optimal policies and interventions [1] [2] [3].

text.text: The Midwest Analytics and Disease Modeling Center's Social Contact Survey (MADMC SCS) was developed to measure contemporary, post-pandemic contact patterns in the upper Midwest, addressing both the lack of sub-national contact data in the United States and the need for updated contact data to reflect post-pandemic behaviors.

The survey collects information about contacts in household, work, school, and community settings, and combines detailed and aggregate reporting to better capture contact patterns of participants with both small and large numbers of contacts.
We use these data to describe sociodemographic variation in daily number of contacts and to generate setting-specific, age-structured contact matrices.
We also assess to what extent Upper Midwest contact patterns differ from national contact data and implication for infectious disease transmission.

The survey was administered online to an opt-in sample recruited by Ipsos, a well-established market research firm with extensive experience conducting opt-in health and behavioral surveys [10] [11] [12] [13].

text.text: The study's target population consisted of non-institutionalized individuals of all ages residing in Minnesota and neighboring states (North and South Dakota, Iowa, and Wisconsin).
The survey was fielded online, in English, between September 14 and October 12, 2025.
Survey respondents who provided a zip code located outside of these states were excluded from the study.
Respondents were also excluded if they took longer than 48 hours to complete the survey or longer than 24 hours and crossing from weekday to weekend or vice versa.
Participants were only allowed to complete the survey once.
Post-stratification weights were provided by the survey vendor to account for study design and to ensure sample representativeness of the upper Midwest region.

Weights were generated to adjust survey responses to match upper Midwest region-specific population distribution by sex, age, race, state of residence, metropolitan status (as defined by the ACS/Office of Budget Management), education level, household income, and employment status, using an iterative proportional fitting (raking) procedure.
Weights also adjusted for days of the week to weight each day of the week equally.
Population targets were obtained from the 2023 American Community Survey [14].

Participation in the MADMC SCS was voluntary.
Consent was obtained from the participant or from the parent or legal guardian of participants under the age of 18 years.

The consenting adult completed the survey on behalf of children 12 years and under, while children aged 13-17 years provided their assent and completed the contact modules of the survey independently after parent/legal guardian consent.
The study was determined to be exempt from human subjects review by the University of Minnesota Institutional Review Board [ID: STUDY0024205].

The survey instrument can be found in Appendix A. We first asked participants about themselves and their household, including questions about age, sex, race/ethnicity, employment, level of education, household income, household size, marital status, and state of residence.
Metropolitan status was determined from participant-reported residential zip code.
Participants were then asked about contacts they had on the previous day.
A contact was defined as a person with whom the participant had an in-person conversation of at least five words or any physical contact (such as a handshake, hug, kiss, or contact sports).
This definition was used to align with other social contact studies [15].
text.formatted: This definition was used to align with other social contact studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: Contact information was obtained separately for four specific settings: household, work, school, and community.
Participants were first asked about their household contacts.
For each household contact, detailed information was collected, including but not limited to the contact's age, sex, and race.

For work, school, and community contacts, participants were first asked to report the total number of contacts in each setting and then asked to list (using pseudonyms or nicknames) up to a maximum of 40 contacts in each setting.

If a participant reported fewer than 10 contacts in a given setting, they were asked to provide detailed information for all of their listed contacts using questions similar to those for household members.
For those reporting more than 10 contacts, detailed information was collected for a random sample of 10 of their listed contacts.
Detailed information was limited to 10 contacts per setting to reduce survey fatigue.

To ensure contact characteristics were still captured for individuals with large numbers of contacts, aggregate information was also collected by asking participants how their remaining contacts were distributed across age groups, allowing for potential imputation of other demographic characteristics.
Community contacts also included a question about how the participant's remaining contacts were distributed across different locations.
Note that setting definitions were based on the participant's relationship to that setting; a participant who worked in a school would report contacts with students and colleagues as work.
We first conducted descriptive analyses of the total number of contacts reported by participants (across all settings).

Participant responses were top-coded (an upward bound to the total number of contacts) at 40 total contacts, similar to other social contact surveys [2, 16, 17], to reduce the influence of outliers on analysis results.

text.text: We examined the distribution of the total number of contacts to assess whether there was evidence of heaping at multiples of 5 or 10, which could indicate participants were loosely estimating rather than re-calling exact number of contacts.

We evaluated how the number of reported contacts varied by participant characteristics, such as sex, age, household size, school attendance (in-person, online, no school), work type (in-person vs. not in-person), household income, residence in a metro area, and day of the week contacts were reported for (weekend vs. weekday).

We used negative binomial regression models to estimate contact rate ratios (RRs) associated with these factors, in both univariate (unadjusted) and multivariate (adjusted) analyses to identify statistically significant differences [13, 16].

text.text: All analyses were conducted using sample weights.

In sensitivity analysis, we ran regression models without top-coding contacts, and we also evaluated the performance of Zero Inflated Poisson and Zero Inflated Negative Binomial regression models in fitting contact data.
Mixing matrices are used to describe how different groups interact with one another and the extent to which contacts are concentrated within groups (homophily or assortativity) versus across groups.

Because age is closely linked with key social contexts such as school, work, and household composition [1], we constructed age-structured mixing matrices to reflect how participants of different ages interact with contacts of different ages.

text.text: We constructed an overall age-structured mixing matrix, as well as separate, setting-specific age-structured matrices for household, work, school, and community.
In the contact data, the maximum number of contacts a participant could have was capped at 40 by location.

text.text: Before comparison, all matrices were harmonized to use the same age-group definitions.
The Epistorm-Mix study included multiple survey waves during the spring, fall, and winter.
To reduce differences that might arise due to seasonality, MADMC SCS results were only compared to the Epistorm-Mix fall 2024 survey results.
We summarized cell-level agreement between MADMC SCS and Epistorm-Mix contact matrices using Pearson's correlation coefficient and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.
To assess the magnitude and direction of the differences, we also calculated the cell-level difference between the MADMC contact matrix and the Epistorm-Mix matrix.

We visualized these differences as heatmaps to identify whether the greatest differences occurred along the main diagonal, between adjacent age groups, or in substantively important off-diagonal cells, such as adult-child contacts.

Finally, to compare transmission potential, we estimated the basic reproduction number (R0) using both the Epistorm-Mix and MADMC contact matrices for a respiratory pathogen assuming uniform susceptibility across age groups [20].

The resulting proportional R0 were then compared to assess differences in transmission potential attributable solely to differences in the contact matrices.

The MADMC SCS analytic sample consisted of 1,009 individuals reporting 5,806 unique contacts (when the maximum number of contacts was top-coded at 40).
Sixty percent (n = 612) of the participants resided in Minnesota and the remaining 40% resided in surrounding states.
Slightly more than half (53%) of our sample was female, and the majority were from metro areas (78%).
Our sample was primarily White (90%); therefore, we did not stratify results by race and ethnicity.
All days of the week were represented in the survey; before applying weights, approximately 23% of participants reported contacts that occurred on a Saturday or Sunday.

text.text: Men reported more contacts than women (RR = 1.28) in the unadjusted results, with a mean of 7.7 (IQR: 2.0-9.0) contacts per day compared to 6.0 (IQR: 1.0-7.0) among women.
This difference was marginally statistically significant in the unadjusted model.
The men in the sample were also more likely to work in person than the women, suggesting that workrelated exposure may partly explain the observed difference.
After adjusting for covariates, men had a lower estimated contact rate than women (RR = 0.91), but this difference was not statistically significant.
The average number of contacts reported per day varied substantially by age.
Contacts were highest among adolescents and young adults, peaking at a mean of 16.
For participants aged 5 -19, most reported contacts took place at school.
After adjustments for covariates, including school attendance and in-person work, age group differences were attenuated.
Participants aged 15-19 remained the most connected (RR = 1.16), followed by those aged 25-30 (Table 2).

Reported contacts increased with household size.
Participants living alone averaged 4.4 contacts per day, while those in two-or three-person households averaged 5.3 to 5.8 contacts per day.
Contact rates were higher in larger households, rising to 8.6 contacts per day among participants in four-person households and 13.8 among those in households with six or more members.
Relative to participants living alone, the difference was statistically significant only for households with more than four members.
After controlling for covariates, only those in households with six or more people had statistically significantly more contacts than those living alone (RR = 1.92).

Participants in households with annual incomes above $100,000 reported more contacts (mean = 7.8-9.3) than those in lower-income households, particularly those earning less than $25,000 (mean = 5.1; IQR: 0.0-5.0) or between $50,000 and $75,000 (mean = 4.2; IQR: 1.0-5.0).
Contact rates did not increase monotonically with household income.
Differences by income were not statistically significant in both unadjusted or adjusted models (p > 0.05).

This difference was not statistically significant in the unadjusted model (RR = 0.87), and controlling for covariates did not materially change the results (RR = 0.94).

Reported contacts were similar on weekdays and weekends.
Participants reported an average of 6.9 contacts per day on weekdays (IQR: 2.0-9.0) and 6.8 contacts per day on weekends (IQR: 2.0-6.0).

When contact counts were analyzed without top-coding, weekend contacts appeared much higher than weekday contacts, however, this difference was no longer statistically significant after adjusting for covariates.

The exception was middle aged participants (40-49) being slightly more likely to interact with children aged 10-19.
Children and young adults exhibited the highest levels of age-assortative mixing, averaging 4 to 7 same age contacts per day.

In the home setting, children and adolescents primarily mixed with siblings, while adults mixed with their similarly aged partners or other household members.
However, the highest number of home contacts reflected inter-generational mixing, particularly between parents aged 30-49 and children aged 0-19.

The Epistorm-Mix data we use had 980 participants with 7,492 contacts.

The maximum number of contacts contributed by a single participant was similar across the two datasets (MADMC SCS: 77; Epistorm-Mix: 67), suggesting that extreme values were unlikely to substantially influence the age-structured contact matrices.
In Epistorm-Mix, 28 participants reported 40 or more contacts, including 9 who reported more than 49 con-tacts.
In comparison, MADMC SCS included 16 participants with 40 or more contacts, of whom only 3 reported more than 49 contacts.
We found a strong statistical correspondence between the national Epistorm-Mix matrix and the MADMC SCS contact matrix (Pearson r= 0.92; Spearman ρ= 0.90; R² = 0.84).
The rank relationship was even stronger when focusing exclusively on the diagonal elements which capture age-assortative mixing (Pearson r= 0.92; Spearman ρ= 0.97).
Despite the overall similarity, the Epistorm-Mix matrix generally exhibited higher contact rates than the MADMC SCS matrix across most age-group pairings.

The primary exception was among younger age groups (<30 years), where MADMC SCS participants reported substantially higher rates of contact within their own age group, reflected in the stronger age-assortative mixing along the matrix diagonal (Figure 3).

The resulting relative R0 (MADMC/Epistorm) was 1.067, indicating that the MADMC SCS contact matrix yielded an R0 6.7% higher than that obtained using the Epistorm contact matrix, holding all other transmission parameters constant.
In the fall of 2025, the MADMC Social Contact Survey recorded an average of 6.8 contacts per day (IQR: 2.0-8.0) among participants in Minnesota and surrounding upper Midwest states.
When we remove the upward bound on number of contacts, the reported mean was 8.7 contacts per day (IQR: 2.0-8.0).

Both estimates fall within the range of recent post-pandemic European estimates of mean daily contacts, including 6.0 contacts per day in Switzerland, 6.5 contacts per day in the United Kingdom, 6.7 contacts per day in Belgium, and 9.9 in the Netherlands [8].

text.text: Our top-coded MADMC SCS estimates were lower than the national US-focused Epistorm-Mix study collected in fall 2024, which estimated 7.4 contacts per day (IQR: 2.0-9.0) nationally and 8.0 contacts per day (IQR: 3.0-10.0) in their Midwestern regional subsample [13].

text.text: However, after removing the top-coding our estimate were slightly higher.

Despite lower total daily contacts than contemporary US national estimates, the Midwest sub-national mixing patterns by age exhibited greater within-age-group transmission potential among children, adolescents, and young adults.
These highly connected age groups can form a transmission "core" that can disproportionately influence epidemic dynamics.
Correspondingly, this difference in age-based mixing resulted in an estimated 6.7% higher R0 than that implied by national contact patterns.

Although modest in relative terms, a difference of this magnitude may still be epidemiologically important when transmission is near the epidemic threshold, where relatively small changes in R0 can substantially alter epi-demic growth rates.

Furthermore, the 6.7% relative difference in R0 is not fixed and could increase or decrease based on interaction between mixing patterns and specific infectious pathogens age pattern of susceptibility and infectiousness.

The observed differences may reflect underlying geographic variation as well as differences in the study period and sampling methodology, particularly the contrast between the probability-based Epistorm-Mix sample and the MADMC SCS opt-in sample.
There were also differences in how MADMC SCS and Epistorm-Mix treated participants with large number of contacts.
As additional national and sub-national data become available, it will be important to assess whether these patterns persist.

Although comparable pre-pandemic estimates of social contact patterns are not avail-able for the Upper Midwest or the United States nationally, MADMC contact rates were approximately half of those reported in historical European studies [2].

text.text: This difference is consistent with broader evidence that the pandemic produced persistent changes in daily routines, including increased work-from-home arrangements.
School and work settings were the primary drivers of social contact patterns.

Consistent with prior research, participants attending school or working in person reported substantially more daily contacts than those who did not, and age groups most engaged in these activities (15-19 and 24-29 years) had the highest contact rates [13].
text.formatted: Consistent with prior research, participants attending school or working in person reported substantially more daily contacts than those who did not, and age groups most engaged in these activities (15-19 and 24-29 years) had the highest contact rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Although individuals in online school also reported high contact rates, most were employed adults whose contacts occurred predominantly in workplaces (Appendix D1).

These findings suggest that continued changes in work arrangements, particularly shifts toward or away from in-person work, could meaningfully affect population-level contact rates and transmission potential.

Higher household income was also associated with greater contact rates, a pattern largely explained by more school-related contacts, including daycare, camp, and after-school care, further underscoring the central role of schools in shaping social mixing (Appendix D2).

At the same time, substantial intergenerational mixing in community settings, particularly between older adults and younger age groups, suggests that community-based interventions may be important for reducing exposure among susceptible older adults.
Additional research is needed to investigate the potential impact of sampling approaches and survey instrument design.
The MADMC social contact survey used an opt-in sample, providing a source of potential bias in the study population.
The post-stratification weights ensured that our sample aligned with key demographic characteristics of the population, but some unobserved differences may still remain.

We were reassured that our findings were consistent with known mixing patterns and that our results were largely consistent with data from Epistorm-Mix, the nationally representative survey that utilized probability sampling.
A second limitation is the reliance on self-reported contact data, which can be subject to reporting bias.

Standard contact survey instruments can be lengthy and burdensome to complete, particularly for individuals with many contacts, and survey fatigue may lead some respondents to under report their true number of interactions.

To assess one potential source of reporting bias, we examined the distribution of reported contacts across all contact modules (home, school, work, and other) for evidence of "heaping" at multiples of 5 and 10.
The resulting histograms showed little evidence of systematic rounding, suggesting that this source of reporting bias was limited (Appendix E).
Nevertheless, further work is needed to identify methods that improve contact ascertainment and reduce under reporting, particularly among highly connected individuals.
Such advances would support more accurate estimates of contact patterns and strengthen inferences about their implications for disease transmission.
In conclusion, contact patterns from the Upper Midwest were similar to national estimates.
However, there were key differences such as higher rates of assortative mixing among participants younger than 30 years of age in the Upper Midwest.
These data are important for better understanding post-pandemic social contact behaviors and potential regional differences that exist.
